title: RBI Kehta Hai — Public Awareness on Banking and Digital Security
passages: RBI Kehta Hai — Digital Payment Safety and UPI PIN Guidelines: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) repeatedly reminds citizens that you need to enter your UPI PIN ONLY when you are SENDING money from your bank account. You NEVER need to enter your UPI PIN or scan a QR code to RECEIVE money. If anyone asks you to enter your UPI PIN or scan a QR code to receive a lottery, refund, or prize money, it is a fraudulent attempt to withdraw money from your account.

RBI Kehta Hai — OTP, CVV and Password Confidentiality: Never share your One Time Password (OTP), Card Verification Value (CVV), ATM PIN, or Internet Banking passwords with anyone over phone, SMS, email, or messaging apps. Bank officials, RBI representatives, and police never ask for your secret PIN or OTP under any circumstance. Beware of fraudulent calls claiming your KYC has expired or your electricity or SIM connection will be disconnected.

RBI Kehta Hai — Reporting Cyber Financial Fraud and Golden Hours: If you become a victim of unauthorized electronic banking transactions or digital financial fraud, report it immediately to your bank and call the National Cyber Crime Helpline number 1930 or file a complaint on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal at cybercrime.gov.in. Reporting unauthorized transactions within the first few hours (golden hours) significantly increases the probability of freezing the stolen funds before fraudsters withdraw them.

RBI Kehta Hai — Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS): The Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme provides a cost-free and expeditious dispute resolution mechanism for customers dissatisfied with banking and financial services. If your bank or regulated entity does not resolve your legitimate complaint within 30 days or rejects it without valid justification, you can escalate your grievance to the RBI Ombudsman via the CMS portal (cms.rbi.org.in).

title: Reserve Bank of India — Monetary Policy, Repo Rate & Deposit Insurance
passages: Reserve Bank of India — Bank Deposit Insurance by DICGC: Under the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC), a wholly owned subsidiary of RBI, each depositor in a registered commercial or cooperative bank is insured up to a maximum limit of Rs 5,00,000 (Rupees Five Lakh) for both principal and interest amounts held in the same capacity and same right across all branches of that bank in case of bank liquidation or cancellation of license.

Reserve Bank of India — Monetary Policy and Inflation Targeting: The primary objective of the Reserve Bank's monetary policy is to maintain price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth. The inflation target under the flexible inflation targeting framework is set at 4% Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation with an allowable tolerance band of +/- 2% (i.e., a range between 2% and 6%). The Policy Repo Rate is the key benchmark interest rate at which the RBI lends short-term liquidity to commercial banks against government securities.

title: SEBI Investor Education — Money Matters, Budgeting & Compounding
passages: SEBI Investor Education — The Power of Compounding and Rule of 72: Compound interest is interest calculated on the initial principal and also on the accumulated interest of previous periods. Albert Einstein famously called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world. The 'Rule of 72' is a simple mental math shortcut: divide 72 by the annual expected rate of return to estimate approximately how many years it will take for your invested money to double. For example, at an 8% annual return, an investment doubles in approximately 72 / 8 = 9 years.

SEBI Investor Education — Building Financial Resilience & Emergency Fund: Before undertaking market investments, an individual should ensure a strong financial foundation: (1) Maintain an emergency fund equivalent to 6 to 12 months of mandatory household expenses in liquid, low-risk instruments such as bank savings or liquid funds; (2) Secure adequate pure term life insurance to protect dependents; and (3) Obtain adequate comprehensive health insurance to prevent medical emergencies from depleting family savings.

SEBI Investor Education — Budgeting with the 50/30/20 Rule: A balanced budgeting approach divides after-tax income into three distinct buckets: 50% for Essential Needs (housing, groceries, utilities, minimum loan obligations), 30% for Discretionary Wants (dining out, entertainment, leisure), and 20% dedicated to Savings and Long-term Investments (emergency fund building, retirement accounts, mutual funds, debt pre-payments).

title: SEBI Investor Education — Personal Investments, Mutual Funds & Asset Allocation
passages: SEBI Investor Education — Mutual Funds Categorization (SEBI Categorization Circular): SEBI categorizes mutual fund schemes into five broad groups to bring uniformity: (1) Equity Schemes (investing primarily in stocks for long-term capital growth, including Large Cap, Mid Cap, Small Cap, Multi Cap, and ELSS); (2) Debt Schemes (investing in fixed-income securities like government bonds, corporate debentures, and treasury bills for capital preservation and steady income); (3) Hybrid Schemes (investing in a mix of equity and debt); (4) Solution Oriented Schemes (Retirement and Children's funds); and (5) Other Schemes (Index Funds and ETFs).

SEBI Investor Education — Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) and Rupee Cost Averaging: A Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) allows an investor to invest a fixed predetermined sum of money at regular intervals (typically monthly) in a mutual fund scheme. SIP instills financial discipline and provides the benefit of Rupee Cost Averaging: when market prices are low, your fixed installment buys more units, and when market prices are high, it buys fewer units, reducing the average purchase cost over time without needing to time the market.

SEBI Investor Education — Asset Allocation and Risk Profiling: Asset allocation is the strategy of dividing an investment portfolio among different asset categories—principally equities, debt/fixed income, gold, and cash equivalents. Because different asset classes react differently to economic events, diversification significantly reduces overall portfolio risk and volatility without necessarily sacrificing long-term returns.

title: SEBI Investor Education — Investor Rights, Dos & Don'ts and SCORES Grievance Redressal
passages: SEBI Investor Education — SEBI Complaints Redress System (SCORES 2.0): SCORES (sebi.gov.in/scores) is a web-based centralized grievance redress system launched by SEBI. It allows retail investors to lodge, track, and follow up on complaints against listed companies, registered brokers, depository participants, mutual funds, and other SEBI-registered intermediaries. Under SCORES guidelines, entities are mandated to address and resolve investor grievances within specified timeframes (typically 21 days).

SEBI Investor Education — Dos and Don'ts for Securities Market Investors: Dos: Always deal only with SEBI-registered intermediaries; verify registration certificates; read offer documents carefully; keep contact information updated with your broker and depository participant. Don'ts: NEVER trade on the basis of unsolicited stock tips, SMS recommendations, or social media groups (Telegram/WhatsApp); never hand over blank signed delivery instruction slips (DIS); and never believe in claims of guaranteed high returns in stock or derivative markets.

title: NCFE — National Centre for Financial Education Core Competencies
passages: NCFE — National Centre for Financial Education 5 Core Competencies: The National Strategy for Financial Education (NSFE) coordinated by NCFE outlines five core financial competencies: (1) Earning (understanding income sources and career capabilities); (2) Spending (distinguishing needs from wants and living within income); (3) Saving (setting aside money regularly for emergency and future goals); (4) Borrowing (responsible credit usage and avoiding high-interest debt traps); and (5) Protecting (managing financial risks through appropriate insurance).

NCFE — Inflation and Purchasing Power Erosion: Inflation is the sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services over time, which reduces the purchasing power of money. If inflation averages 6% annually, a basket of essential goods costing Rs 100 today will cost approximately Rs 179 in ten years. Therefore, savings must be invested in assets that have the potential to earn returns beating inflation after taxes to avoid real wealth erosion.

title: NCFE — National Financial Literacy Assessment Test (NFLAT) Guidelines
passages: NCFE — National Financial Literacy Assessment Test (NFLAT): NFLAT is a nationwide financial literacy assessment initiative designed to measure and promote basic financial education and money management awareness among school and college students across India. It evaluates fundamental conceptual knowledge in banking, savings, basic securities markets, insurance, pension products, and digital payment security.
